name: Pi-hole
description: Network-wide ad and tracker blocking DNS server with a web dashboard. Installed without changing any DNS setting of this PC or your network.

inputs.label: Answer DNS for other devices (port 53 on this PC)
inputs.help: Off: the dashboard works, but no device uses Pi-hole. On: port 53 must be free; you then point devices or your router at this PC yourself.

security: Installing changes no DNS setting: not on this PC, not on your router. Using Pi-hole is a separate decision you make on each device or on the router.
If this PC sleeps or Docker stops, devices that use it as DNS lose name resolution.

notes: The dashboard has its own password. Its API (/api) is used by apps and widgets that ForwardAuth would block; DNS itself is not HTTP and is unaffected.

limitations: Docker Desktop puts DNS clients behind its network proxy: queries may all appear to come from one address, so per-device statistics and DHCP do not work.
Port 53 can be in use on Windows (Internet Connection Sharing, Hyper-V DNS proxy); the plan checks it before installing.
For a household DNS server, an always-on Linux host or Raspberry Pi is more reliable than a Windows desktop.
manualSetup: Sign in to the dashboard at /admin with the password from credentials.txt.
Only if you want Pi-hole to filter: enable port 53, then set this PC's address as the DNS server on one test device before changing your router.

update.notes: Gravity (blocklists) updates itself weekly inside the container; the image changes only with a catalog update.

testStatus.notes: Installed in isolation: health, own API, network isolation, modular stack, stop/start, Traefik file route, backup and restore, removal with data.
